subject: iot
title: Unit 1 MCQs — Introduction to IoT & Architecture

items.q: Which set best captures the four core concepts that almost every IoT system rests on?
items.explain: The four pillars are connectivity (reach the internet), sensing (capture the physical world), communication (exchange data via MQTT/CoAP/HTTP), and analytics (turn data into decisions).

items.q: A 'smart object' is distinguished from an ordinary electronic device primarily because it can:
options: Sense, process, communicate, and (often) actuate — acting on data autonomously
Only display a numeric reading to a human
items.explain: A smart object adds sensing, embedded processing, network communication, and often actuation — enabling the sense → communicate → analyse → act loop with little human intervention.

items.q: Who coined the term 'Internet of Things', and in what context?
options: Tim Berners-Lee, while inventing the web
Kevin Ashton (1999, MIT Auto-ID Center), in the context of RFID supply-chain tracking
Mark Weiser, in his ubiquitous-computing paper
items.explain: Kevin Ashton coined 'Internet of Things' in 1999 at MIT's Auto-ID Center; the original driver was using RFID to let systems track physical goods without human data entry.

items.q: Which of these is frequently cited as the first internet-connected appliance?
items.explain: The early-1980s Carnegie Mellon Coke machine, wired to the ARPANET so students could check stock and temperature remotely, is widely cited as the first internet-connected appliance.

items.q: Compared with human-generated internet traffic, IoT-generated traffic is typically:
options: Downlink-heavy and bursty during the day
Uplink-heavy, event-based or periodic, and mostly stationary
Always large in volume and highly mobile
Identical in pattern to human web browsing
items.explain: Humans are data consumers (downlink-heavy, daytime peaks); IoT devices are data producers (uplink-heavy), event-based/periodic, and mostly stationary.

items.q: A smoke-detector alarm's traffic is best characterised as:
items.explain: A smoke alarm fires rarely (event-based) but the alert must arrive fast (low latency) and be confirmed (ACK) — small data, high urgency.

items.q: Why can a smart meter's tiny power-outage notification be more important than its routine consumption data?
options: Because it is much larger in size
Because urgency is about latency and reliability, not data volume
Because routine data is never transmitted
items.explain: Importance in IoT is driven by latency and reliability requirements, not byte count. A few-byte outage alert is urgent; megabytes of routine telemetry can be best-effort.

items.q: Which technology best fits a long-range, very-low-power, low-data-rate use case such as remote agricultural sensors?
items.explain: LoRaWAN (an LPWAN) offers long range and very low power at low data rates — ideal for remote, battery-powered sensors that send small amounts of data.

items.q: What does LPWAN stand for, and what is its defining trade-off?
options: Low-Power Wide-Area Network — long range and low power at the cost of low data rate
Local Private Wireless Access Node — high bandwidth, short range
Low-Priority Wide-Access Network — best-effort cloud access
Large-Payload Wireless Area Network — high data rate, high power
items.explain: LPWANs (LoRaWAN, NB-IoT, Sigfox) trade bandwidth for long range and multi-year battery life — matching the uplink-light, periodic traffic of most sensors.

items.q: Why do short-range, non-IP devices (e.g., Zigbee/BLE sensors) require an IoT gateway?
options: Because they generate too little data to be useful
Because the gateway performs protocol translation to IP-friendly formats, aggregation, edge processing, and security
Because gateways increase their battery life directly
Because IP devices are not allowed on the internet
items.explain: Short-range/non-IP devices can't reach the internet alone. The gateway bridges them — translating protocols (to HTTP/MQTT/CoAP), aggregating data, doing edge processing, and enforcing security.

items.q: Which is NOT a typical function of an IoT gateway?
options: Protocol translation between non-IP and IP networks
Training large deep-learning models on years of historical data
items.explain: Heavy model training is a cloud function (massive compute, long-term data). Gateways translate protocols, aggregate, do lightweight edge processing, and enforce security.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes digitization from digital transformation?
options: Digitization converts analog info/processes to digital form; digital transformation is the broader business change it enables
Digitization is a business strategy; digital transformation is a sensor type
items.explain: Digitization = analog → digital (e.g., sensors replacing a paper log). Digital transformation = the resulting business change (predictive maintenance, new business models).

items.q: Most IoT devices predominantly produce which kind of data, well-suited to AI?
items.explain: IoT sensors emit timestamped readings sampled repeatedly — time-series data — which suits forecasting, anomaly detection, and predictive maintenance.

items.q: What is the difference between a horizontal IoT platform and an IoT vertical?
options: Horizontal = a single device; vertical = a single sensor
Horizontal = cross-industry foundation (cloud, analytics, security); vertical = an industry-specific end-use domain
items.explain: Horizontal platforms provide reusable, cross-industry infrastructure; verticals are the industry domains (healthcare, manufacturing…) where tailored solutions create real impact.

items.q: Industrial IoT (IIoT) is often called the backbone of:
items.explain: IIoT integrates sensors, machines, and analytics across manufacturing and utilities — the foundation of Industry 4.0's cyber-physical, data-driven factories.

items.q: Why is predictive maintenance generally superior to reactive and preventive maintenance?
options: It repairs equipment exactly when sensor data indicates need — avoiding both breakdowns and unnecessary early servicing
It schedules repairs on a fixed calendar regardless of condition
It only fixes machines after they fail
items.explain: Reactive fixes after failure (costly downtime); preventive services on a calendar (often too early/late); predictive uses live data to act exactly when needed — the cost sweet spot.

items.q: In smart healthcare, IoMT stands for the Internet of Medical Things, and its key sub-domain RPM means:
options: Remote Patient Monitoring — continuous tracking of vitals via wearable/in-home devices
items.explain: RPM (Remote Patient Monitoring) uses wearables (ECG, glucometers, SpO₂) to stream vitals to providers, enabling early intervention without hospitalisation.

items.q: The smart-farming 'data → action' loop proceeds in which order?
options: Data collection → Diagnostics → Decision-making → Action (then repeat)
items.explain: Sensors collect data → the system diagnoses problems → software/human decides actions → actions execute and sensors re-measure, restarting the cycle.

items.q: In connected vehicles, 'V2X' communication includes which of the following?
items.explain: V2X ('vehicle-to-everything') spans V2V and V2I, letting cars share location/hazard info so they effectively 'see around corners' before line-of-sight.

items.q: The 2016 Mirai incident is a classic example of which IoT challenge?
options: Security & privacy — IoT devices with default credentials hijacked into a DDoS botnet
items.explain: Mirai conscripted IoT devices left on default passwords into a massive DDoS botnet — the textbook example of weak IoT device security endangering whole networks.

items.q: The fact that one device may speak MQTT, another CoAP, and a third a proprietary API illustrates which challenge?
options: Lack of interoperability / standards (leading to vendor lock-in)
items.explain: With no universal IoT protocol, multi-vendor devices struggle to interoperate, causing integration complexity, fragmentation, and vendor lock-in.

items.q: For battery-powered sensors in hard-to-reach locations, the central power-management trade-off is between:
options: CPU clock speed and RAM size
Number of buttons and case color
items.explain: Every transmission drains the battery, so devices balance how often they send against how long they last — often batching and sleeping to extend lifetime.

items.q: An 'architectural driver' in IoT is best described as:
options: A physical hardware component such as a sensor
A force, goal, or constraint (technical/economic/user) that shapes the architecture
A device driver in the operating system
items.explain: Drivers are not components but requirements/constraints — e.g., low latency forces edge computing; massive scale forces microservices.

items.q: Which driver most directly forces the adoption of edge computing?
items.explain: When milliseconds decide safety, a cloud round-trip is too slow, so processing must move to the edge near the data source.

items.q: Which correctly distinguishes horizontal from vertical scaling?
options: Horizontal = make one machine bigger; vertical = add more machines
Horizontal = add more machines/nodes (scale out); vertical = make one machine bigger (scale up)
items.explain: Horizontal scaling adds nodes (scale out); vertical scaling upgrades a single machine (scale up). IoT favours horizontal scaling for millions of devices.

items.q: In the classic 3-layer IoT architecture, which layer contains the sensors and RFID that gather data from the environment?
items.explain: The perception (physical) layer senses the environment and identifies smart objects; the network layer transports data; the application layer delivers services.

items.q: What does the 5-layer model add over the 3-layer model?
options: It inserts data-processing (middleware) and service/business layers for finer separation of analytics and logic
It merges all layers into one
It only renames the application layer
items.explain: The 5-layer model keeps perception → network → application and inserts a data-processing/middleware layer (the 'brain') and a service/business layer, making analytics and business logic explicit.

items.q: Which architecture style is the best fit when interoperability across many vendors is the dominant requirement?
options: Middleware-based architecture (e.g., a common service layer like oneM2M)
items.explain: A middleware layer standardises communication and abstracts hardware so multi-vendor devices interoperate — exactly what oneM2M provides.

items.q: A continuously-updated virtual replica of a physical asset, used for simulation and predictive maintenance, is a:
items.explain: A digital twin mirrors a real asset's live sensor data, letting you simulate scenarios and predict failures on the copy without touching the original.

items.q: In oneM2M, which entity is the core 'common service layer' providing registration, security, and data management?
items.explain: The CSE is the heart of oneM2M, offering reusable services; it is deployed as IN-CSE (cloud), MN-CSE (gateway), or on a device node. The AE holds application logic; the NSE interfaces the telecom network.

items.q: An MN-CSE (Middle Node CSE) in oneM2M is typically deployed at the:
items.explain: IN-CSE lives in the cloud, MN-CSE at the gateway/fog/edge, and the application/device node on the device itself — the same CSE services at each tier enable interoperability.

items.q: In the Cisco IoTWF reference model, security and management are:
options: A single layer at the very top
Cross-cutting concerns that span all layers
Only present in the perception layer
items.explain: IoTWF applies security and management across every layer (cross-cutting), not as one isolated layer — protecting and operating the whole device-to-business stack.

items.q: In the Core IoT Functional Stack's Communications Network layer, which sublayer is the 'final segment' that sensors actually attach to (e.g., 802.15.4g, LoRa)?
items.explain: The access network is the last hop to the device. The gateways/backhaul sublayer aggregates it; network transport runs IP/UDP; IoT network management runs CoAP/MQTT.

items.q: Which placement is correct for an autonomous drone that must avoid obstacles in real time?
options: Cloud — send video to a remote data centre and wait for a decision
Edge — process locally on-device for ultra-low latency and offline autonomy
Fog only — rely entirely on a LAN gateway kilometres away
items.explain: Obstacle avoidance needs millisecond reactions and must work even without connectivity, so it belongs at the edge (on-device), not via a cloud round-trip.

items.q: Which tier of the compute stack is best suited to training a predictive-maintenance ML model on a year of fleet data?
items.explain: Heavy analytics, long-term petabyte-scale storage, and global data fusion are cloud strengths; edge handles real-time reflexes and fog handles site-level aggregation.
